# Taken Over by Views

*Iti 49, the Diṭṭhigata Sutta — set 4, Not-Self and Dependent Arising*

<p class="reading-meta"><strong>Reading time:</strong> about 2 min · 310 words</p>

[Skip to the translation](#translation){ .reader-skip-link }

## Before you read

This short text names two ways a view can take over. One side clings to
continued becoming. The other is so disgusted by becoming that it treats the
destruction of a self after death as peace.

The Buddha does not ask you to pick one of those positions. The practical
alternative is to notice what has come to be, see it without turning it into
something permanent, and let fascination with it fade. The closing verse is
compact, but its point is direct: freedom is not wanting either to keep
becoming or to be wiped out.

## Translation

### Two Ways Views Take Over

This was said by the Buddha, said by the arahant—so I heard:

"Bhikkhus, gods and humans are taken over by two views. Some hold back, while
others go too far. Those who see clearly recognize what is happening.

### Holding Back

"How do some hold back?

"Gods and humans delight in becoming. They enjoy it and celebrate it. So when
the Dhamma for the quenching of becoming is taught, their hearts do not take
to it, grow confident in it, settle on it, or commit to it.

"This is how some hold back.

### Going Too Far

"And how do some go too far?

"Some are distressed, ashamed, and disgusted by becoming itself. They welcome
non-becoming, thinking:

"'When the body breaks up after death, this self is cut off, destroyed, and no
longer exists. This is peaceful. This is excellent. This is how things really
are.'

"This is how some go too far.

### Seeing Clearly

"And how do those who see clearly recognize what is happening?

"Here a bhikkhu sees what has come to be simply as what has come to be. Seeing
it this way, they practice for disenchantment with it, for its fading, and for
its quenching.

"This is how those who see clearly recognize what is happening."

This is what the Buddha said. And in reference to this, it was said:

### Verses

"Those who see what has come to be
simply as what has come to be,
and see the way beyond it,
are released in line with reality
when ignorant wanting for becoming is completely worn away.

"Fully understanding what has come to be,
free of wanting for becoming or non-becoming,
a bhikkhu does not come to further becoming
when what has come to be is gone."

This too was said by the Buddha—so I heard.

The twelfth discourse is finished.

<dd>Someone who has completed the path and has nothing further to do. Left untranslated; &quot;saint&quot; and &quot;perfected one&quot; both mislead.</dd>
<dt><dfn>bhikkhu</dfn></dt>
<dd>A Buddhist monk -- someone who has left household life to practise full time. Left untranslated because &quot;monk&quot; carries centuries of unrelated European associations.</dd>
<dt><dfn>bhikkhus</dfn></dt>
<dd>Buddhist monks -- those who have left household life to practise full time. The Buddha&#x27;s usual way of addressing the assembly, roughly &quot;friends&quot; in force.</dd>
<dt><dfn>body</dfn></dt>
<dd>The physical body, as distinct from speech and the mental side of experience.</dd>
<dt><dfn>Dhamma</dfn></dt>
<dd>The Buddha&#x27;s teaching taken as a whole -- both what he taught and the way things actually are, which the teaching describes.</dd>
<dt><dfn>disenchantment</dfn></dt>
<dd>A cooling of fascination with ordinary experience -- not depression, but the natural next step once you see clearly how things actually work.</dd>
<dt><dfn>fading</dfn></dt>
<dd>The fading away of attraction and investment in experience, as passion cools.</dd>
<dt><dfn>ignorant wanting</dfn></dt>

*[arahant]: Someone who has completed the path and has nothing further to do. Left untranslated; "saint" and "perfected one" both mislead.
*[bhikkhu]: A Buddhist monk -- someone who has left household life to practise full time. Left untranslated because "monk" carries centuries of unrelated European associations.
*[body]: The physical body, as distinct from speech and the mental side of experience.
*[Dhamma]: The Buddha's teaching taken as a whole -- both what he taught and the way things actually are, which the teaching describes.
*[disenchantment]: A cooling of fascination with ordinary experience -- not depression, but the natural next step once you see clearly how things actually work.
*[fading]: The fading away of attraction and investment in experience, as passion cools.
*[ignorant wanting]: This project's rendering of "taṇhā" (often translated "craving"), chosen to keep visible that the wanting in question is driven by not seeing clearly, not just ordinary desire.
*[quenching]: An extinguishing image for dissatisfaction and its causes going out. Different Pali words use this image on different pages, so the exact scope comes from the sentence.
